name: Dirty Orange
lede: Dirty Orange is a deep, muted orange named by the 2010 xkcd color survey, close enough to the Japanese traditional color Yamabukicha to carry its own "in Japan" thread.

sections.title: A plain English name, a Japanese echo
sections.body:
The English name is a straightforward xkcd-survey label from 2010, duller than plain orange [1]. Ridgway's 1912 plate III, hue 15, tone i, independently recorded a close match, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 filed the same region into block 50, named strong orange in that system's own list [1]. Our library also records a near-duplicate, Mars Yellow, about 1.5 units off, from the same two older sources [1].

**In Japan**, the nearest traditional record is Yamabukicha (山吹茶), "gold-brown", named for the kerria rose, or yamabuki; our data flags it as a near match in hex, not a claim that the English and Japanese names share an origin [1]. Its closest look-alike on file is [[ochre]], about 3.0 units off, with [[xanthine-orange]], [[brown-orange]] and [[copper]] close behind [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 1.02% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (243 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 203 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 71% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1800s, present in 1.1% of the 8,345 paintings we have from that decade (90 paintings), 1.3 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 82% of its 203 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is George Dawe, present in 12 of 50 works here, 10.1x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 11.8x) [3]. It is most over-represented in India, 3.1x expected (17 of 721 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1290, 622 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
